strengths: The manuscript presents a clear, practically motivated idea: learn per-head sensitivity to restricted KV access through RL, then retain full caches only for the highest-ranked heads. The small L×H optimization space makes the approach technically plausible. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2e40aee00006402798b8dfb099e503a1/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation covers two model families, three mathematical benchmarks, and an out-of-domain coding benchmark. Tables 3–4 show that RLKV generally degrades more gracefully than H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention, especially at moderate sparsity.

The ablations examine adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, and the L1 coefficient. The controlled head-replacement analysis is also useful evidence that the learned ranking captures heads whose cache access materially affects task accuracy.
The paper is generally well organized, explains the motivation and training-collapse problem clearly, and provides many implementation hyperparameters in Appendix A.2.
weaknesses: Soundness: the evidence does not justify the strong functional interpretation of dedicated “reasoning heads.” RLKV defines important heads through preservation of reasoning-task reward, and Figure 6 then shows that heads selected by this objective are important under the same type of intervention. This is partly circular and does not distinguish reasoning-specific function from general next-token prediction, long-range attention, answer formatting, or task-specific importance.

The claimed improvements lack uncertainty estimates. RL training is stochastic, but only one run is reported, with no seed-to-seed stability of accuracy or selected heads. This is especially problematic for AIME24: its 30 examples mean the highlighted +3.3 and +6.7 point improvements correspond to only one and two additional correct answers.

Possible train–test contamination is not addressed. Training problems are sampled from DeepScaleR, but the paper does not report deduplication against GSM8K, MATH500, or AIME24. Filtering to problems each evaluated model already solves can further bias the selected training distribution.

The practical efficiency claim is inadequately supported. Section 4.4 reports task accuracy at nominal cache sparsities but no measured peak GPU memory, throughput, latency, kernel overhead, or batch-size improvement. Consequently, statements about GPU-memory reduction, higher parallelism, and deployability are projections from KV allocation rather than demonstrated system-level results.

Comparison details remain ambiguous. Training uses 128 sink plus 256 local tokens whereas inference uses 16 plus 64; the precise accounting that maps head sparsity and these fixed windows to an equal total KV budget for token-dropping baselines is not formalized. Baselines also use eager attention while RLKV and DuoAttention use FlashAttention, preventing meaningful runtime comparison.

Generality is limited to two closely related 7–8B distilled reasoning models. There is no evaluation on larger models, non-distilled reasoning models, non-mathematical training data, standard long-context retrieval tasks, or evidence that learned head rankings transfer across datasets, context lengths, or checkpoints.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or learned head masks are supplied; training cost and wall-clock time are omitted; several framework and baseline choices are deferred to “default” or “recommended” settings; and exact reward checking, error-mode classification rules, and random seeds are insufficiently specified.

Presentation and limitations: several multi-panel figures are difficult to read at normal scale, and the error analyses do not give category counts or operational definitions precise enough to reproduce them. The future-work section does not candidly discuss the key limitations above. Ethical risk is relatively low, and the LLM-use declaration is welcome, but compute/environmental cost and risks of interpreting correlational head rankings mechanistically are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and increasingly important bottleneck: KV-cache growth during long chain-of-thought generation. Per-head cache allocation is a useful direction because it is complementary to quantization and system-level memory optimizations.

The proposed method is technically plausible and lightweight: only L×H gating parameters are optimized while model weights remain frozen. The adaptive penalty and curriculum-style sampling directly address an observed optimization collapse, and the ablations provide evidence that both components matter.

The empirical results show a meaningful advantage at moderate sparsity. Across two 7B–8B reasoning models and four math/code benchmarks, RLKV generally preserves accuracy better than H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention. Generalization from mathematical training data to MBPP is especially encouraging.

The head-replacement intervention is more informative than a purely correlational visualization: compressing highly ranked RLKV heads hurts performance more than compressing random or DuoAttention-ranked heads. The manuscript is also visually polished and provides full result tables, implementation hardware, major hyperparameters, and an LLM-use declaration.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is substantially stronger than the evidence. The learned scores identify heads whose full-cache access helps preserve task accuracy under one particular streaming-attention perturbation; this does not establish that they are functionally distinct “reasoning heads.” The paper provides no mechanistic analysis, ranking stability across training seeds, overlap across tasks/models, transfer of rankings between reasoning domains, or tests separating reasoning from other long-sequence functions. The top-head compression experiment largely verifies the sensitivity criterion used to learn the ranking.

Claims of near-lossless 20–50% compression are not statistically supported. Results come from one RL training run and one greedy evaluation, with no uncertainty estimates or seed analysis. This is particularly problematic for AIME24, which has only 30 problems: reported changes of 3.3 or 6.7 points correspond to one or two examples and cannot support claims that compression improves reasoning or removes noisy heads. “Lossless” is also not formally defined and includes degradations as large as 1.8 points.

The practical efficiency claim is inadequately evaluated. No measured peak memory, throughput, latency, kernel overhead, batch-size gain, or training cost is reported. “KV cache budget sparsity” is not translated into exact end-to-end memory savings, despite compressed heads retaining sink and recent tokens and training using a different local-cache size from inference. Consequently, the claim of 20–50% GPU-memory reduction is essentially inferred rather than demonstrated.

The evaluation is narrow for a claimed state-of-the-art compression method: it covers only two closely related small distilled models, three math benchmarks, and one code benchmark. It omits larger models, other architectures, long-context retrieval or language modeling, realistic serving workloads, and several head-reallocation baselines discussed in related work. The baseline implementations are modified to use dynamic budgets, but the precise equal-memory accounting is not provided.

Performance at aggressive compression is poor and some summary language is inaccurate. At 0.6 sparsity, RLKV loses 5–30 points on many settings; at 0.8, most tasks nearly collapse. RLKV also does not consistently beat every baseline—for example, R-KV is better on Llama GSM8K at 0.8 and DuoAttention is better on Llama and Qwen MBPP at 0.8. The selected “lossless sparsity thresholds” obscure this broader behavior.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although several hyperparameters are listed, the manuscript does not provide code, learned head rankings/checkpoints, adapter initialization, the GRPO clipping value, handling of zero-variance reward groups, exact reward and answer-checking procedures, training time, random seeds, or sufficiently precise specifications for the modified baselines and error-mode classification.

The presentation is generally clear, but causal conclusions repeatedly exceed the experiments—for example, improvements over the full-cache baseline are attributed to non-reasoning heads introducing noise, and error patterns are taken to imply collaborative maintenance of logical states. These are hypotheses, not demonstrated findings. The paper also lacks a candid limitations section addressing model scale, statistical uncertainty, selection bias from self-filtered training data, and the gap between cache-size proxies and actual serving efficiency. No major ethical issue is apparent, but data licensing and broader deployment considerations are not discussed.

strengths: Soundness: The method is coherent: per-head gates interpolate full and streaming attention, GRPO optimizes answer-based rewards, and L1 regularization induces a ranking that supports multiple cache budgets. Stabilization components are motivated and ablated.

Evaluation: Experiments cover two reasoning models, four math/code benchmarks, four sparsity levels, and three relevant baselines. Detailed numerical results generally show RLKV outperforming competing methods, especially at moderate compression.

Significance: Preserving reasoning performance while reducing KV-cache use by roughly 20–50% is practically useful for long-chain-of-thought inference, where memory limits batch size and deployability.

Originality: Using generation-level reinforcement-learning feedback to identify cache-sensitive heads is a meaningful departure from retrieval- or single-forward-pass-based head selection. The distinction between reasoning-oriented and retrieval-oriented allocations is interesting.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, visually readable, and provides useful implementation details, full result tables, error-mode analyses, and component ablations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the proposed efficiency technique.
weaknesses: The term “reasoning heads” is stronger than the evidence supports. The method identifies heads whose full cache improves final-answer reward under a particular streaming-attention intervention; this does not establish that these heads specifically implement reasoning rather than broader long-range attention or task-dependent functions. The head-removal analysis is partly circular because importance is evaluated using the same type of intervention used to learn the ranking.

Empirical uncertainty is not quantified: results appear to use one training run and greedy evaluation without seeds, confidence intervals, or variance across training runs. This is particularly consequential for AIME24, where increments of 3.3 percentage points correspond to a single problem, making claims that compression removes harmful “noise” unsupported.

The systems contribution is incompletely validated. The paper reports nominal KV-cache sparsity but no measured peak GPU memory, throughput, latency, or batch-capacity improvements. Consequently, the practical deployment claims are plausible but not directly demonstrated, and comparisons using eager attention for some baselines versus FlashAttention for RLKV would complicate any unstated runtime comparison.

Baseline coverage is limited relative to the related-work discussion: Ada-KV, RazorAttention, and PruLong are omitted, leaving only one head-reallocation baseline. The paper also modifies token-dropping baselines to use dynamic budgets, but does not sufficiently validate that these adaptations preserve their intended operating behavior.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Hyperparameters and hardware are reported, but the manuscript does not provide code, learned head masks, random seeds, exact checkpoint identifiers for all models, training cost, reward-verification details, GRPO clipping parameters, or handling of zero reward variance. The use of different local windows during training (128+256 tokens) and evaluation (16+64) also needs justification.

The “lossless sparsity threshold” is not formally defined and appears selected separately for each benchmark; several labeled near-lossless settings still lose 0.8–1.8 points. The paper should predefine a tolerance and account for statistical uncertainty. Its limitations discussion also understates the narrow scope: only two related 7–8B distilled models, math-only training data, short benchmark suites, and no leakage analysis for the filtered DeepScaleR training set. Minor inconsistencies such as AIME24 versus AIME25 further reduce precision.

strengths: Soundness: The core allocation method is plausible and well motivated: lightweight per-head gates mix full and local attention, GRPO optimizes them using outcome rewards, and sparsity regularization produces a deployable head ranking while freezing the base model.

Evidence: Evaluation covers three reasoning models, four reasoning benchmarks, and four MMLU-Pro subsets. The complete tables show that RLKV generally offers a better accuracy–compression trade-off than H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention, especially at moderate sparsity.

The paper includes useful ablations of adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, and regularization strength, plus head-sensitivity and error-mode analyses that support the practical value of the learned ranking.

Significance: Preserving reasoning quality under KV-cache compression is an important inference problem. The reported 20–50% cache reductions and 1.09–1.21× end-to-end speedups suggest useful practical benefits, even if the systems evidence remains preliminary.
Originality: Using outcome-based reinforcement learning as a probe for head-level cache allocation is a novel and interesting extension beyond retrieval-oriented head-selection criteria.

Presentation is generally clear and organized, with full numerical results, training costs, hyperparameters, baseline adjustments, and an impact statement. Freezing the underlying model and training only gates keeps the identification cost relatively modest.
weaknesses: The mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the evidence. “Reasoning-critical” is operationally defined as sensitivity to one particular local-cache perturbation, and the gates are trained explicitly to preserve task reward under that perturbation. This demonstrates an effective allocation policy, but not that the selected heads intrinsically maintain reasoning consistency or control termination. Head interactions, redundancy, causal interventions, and alternative compression operators are not studied.

Statistical evidence is limited. There are no confidence intervals, repeated training runs, or head-ranking stability measurements. This matters particularly for AIME24, where 3.3 and 6.7 percentage-point changes correspond to only one and two questions, respectively. Random-head controls also lack reported variability.

Several important design details remain insufficiently specified for reproduction, including gate parameterization and initialization, checkpoint/package versions, exact model identifiers in some cases, random seeds, learned head rankings, and how deployment thresholds are selected. No code or released artifacts are identified.

The efficiency claim is evaluated only for Llama-3.1-8B-R1 on Math500 in a vanilla implementation. Table 2 changes batch size between full-cache and RLKV conditions, reports aggregate latency rather than token-normalized throughput, and does not compare against DuoAttention or other baselines under matched serving conditions. Thus, the practical 1.09–1.21× speedup is suggestive but not yet a comprehensive systems result.

The meaning and implementation of “KV cache budget sparsity” and the fixed-versus-dynamic baseline budgets are unnecessarily ambiguous. The appendix alternates between budgets based on evolving sequence length and budgets derived from full-model response length; explicit online algorithms and realized per-example memory statistics are needed to rule out oracle information or mismatched compression rates.

Training uses 3,000 model-solvable DeepScaleR math problems selected partly by response length. The paper does not audit overlap with math evaluation sets or analyze how filtering affects the learned heads. MBPP and MMLU-Pro provide encouraging transfer evidence, but stability across training corpora, domains, prompts, and checkpoints is not established.

Ablations are confined largely to Qwen-2.5-7B-R1 on Math500, despite model-dependent behavior such as the limited sparsification of that model. The training/evaluation local-window mismatch (128+256 tokens during training versus 16+64 during evaluation) is also not isolated.

“Near-lossless” is not formally defined and includes drops as large as 3.2 percentage points in Table 1. Some figures are very dense, and several substantive limitations—per-model RL cost, static rankings, small-model scope, benchmark contamination risk, and lack of production-engine integration—are deferred to future work rather than treated explicitly as limitations. Ethical risks are low, but the impact discussion is correspondingly generic.

strengths: Originality/significance: Using outcome-driven reinforcement learning to rank KV heads for reasoning workloads is a novel and practically relevant extension of head-reallocation compression. The distinction between retrieval-oriented and reasoning-oriented head selection is insightful.

Empirical scope: The evaluation covers three reasoning models, mathematics, coding, and four MMLU-Pro domains, four sparsity levels, and three representative baselines. The complete numerical tables generally show that RLKV improves the accuracy–compression trade-off, especially around 40–60% sparsity.

Analysis: The head-sensitivity, response-length, and failure-mode studies provide useful qualitative evidence beyond aggregate accuracy. The comparison with instruct variants also motivates why reasoning generation presents a distinct compression challenge.

Practicality: Only per-head gates are trained while model weights remain frozen. The paper reports training cost, hardware, major hyperparameters, local-cache sizes, and actual end-to-end measurements rather than only theoretical KV savings.

Ethics/limitations: The work raises no major research-ethics concern. The impact statement acknowledges possible downstream accuracy degradation, and the future-work discussion honestly identifies static head allocation and the lack of specialized kernels as limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central mechanistic claim that the method discovers heads that are specifically “essential for reasoning” is stronger than the evidence. The operational definition merely identifies heads whose compression hurts task reward. Such heads could support generic long-context retention, generation stability, or answer formatting rather than reasoning itself. No non-reasoning matched controls, interventions on particular reasoning behaviors, or cross-task transfer tests disentangle these explanations.

The head-sensitivity experiment is partly circular: the gates are optimized so that high-scoring heads preserve reward under the chosen local-attention intervention, and the analysis then shows that compressing those same high-scoring heads hurts reward. Held-out tasks make this useful validation for compression, but not compelling evidence of a distinct reasoning mechanism.

Statistical reliability is insufficient. Results appear to come from one training run per model, with no seeds, variance, confidence intervals, or stability analysis of the selected heads. This is especially problematic for AIME24, which has only 30 examples: reported gains of 3.3 or 6.7 points correspond to only one or two problems and cannot support robust superiority claims.

The claimed 20–50% “near-lossless” range is selectively summarized and uses task-dependent thresholds without a clearly stated tolerance. At several reported settings RLKV still loses multiple accuracy points, while the improvements over full-cache inference are treated as meaningful despite absent uncertainty estimates.

The efficiency evidence is difficult to interpret. Table 2 compares full-cache and RLKV runs at different batch sizes, labels a large aggregate quantity simply as “latency,” and reports accuracy changing with batch size despite greedy decoding. It does not compare end-to-end speed against compression baselines. Peak total GPU memory is nearly unchanged in the paired rows, so the practical memory and latency claims need clearer measurement definitions and controlled comparisons.

Baseline comparability is not fully established. H2O and R-KV are modified to use a dynamic, growing budget plus added sink/local tokens, whereas DuoAttention and RLKV use FlashAttention and the token-dropping methods use eager attention. Accuracy comparisons may remain informative, but these implementation differences preclude a unified systems-efficiency conclusion.

The ablations are limited to one model and one benchmark and are presented only as plots without uncertainty. There is no comparison against simpler head-ranking objectives, such as supervised answer loss, likelihood preservation on generated traces, or direct gate optimization without GRPO, so it remains unclear whether reinforcement learning itself supplies the claimed benefit.

Reproducibility is only partial. Although many hyperparameters and GPU-hour costs are provided, the manuscript gives no code-release statement and omits random seeds, gate initialization, precise reward/checker and answer-normalization logic, exact GRPO defaults, head-selection rounding details, and sufficient information to reproduce the latency measurements.

Presentation is generally organized, but several main-paper figures contain many very small subplots and are hard to read. Terminology such as “KV cache budget sparsity” and the fixed-versus-dynamic budget discussion is unnecessarily confusing, and some claims of consistent superiority overlook settings where DuoAttention is better.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical result is compelling. Across three reasoning models, eight evaluation domains, and four compression levels, RLKV generally provides the best accuracy–memory trade-off; the complete tables show especially consistent gains over H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention at moderate sparsity.

Originality: Using outcome-based reinforcement learning to learn head-level cache allocation is a novel and well-motivated departure from attention-score heuristics or retrieval-head identification. The mixed-attention gates provide a lightweight optimization space while leaving model weights frozen.

Significance: Preserving reasoning quality under 20–50% KV-cache reduction is practically useful. The reported 1.09–1.21× end-to-end speedup at approximately matched peak memory demonstrates that the method offers some realized benefit rather than only theoretical compression.

Evaluation breadth is strong: results cover mathematics at several difficulty levels, code generation, and four MMLU-Pro subjects. Generalization from mathematical gate training to code and knowledge tasks is particularly encouraging.

Presentation and analysis: The paper is generally clear and well organized. Ablations examine adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, and regularization strength; head-sensitivity and error-mode analyses also help explain why retrieval-oriented allocation is insufficient.

Ethics and limitations: The impact statement appropriately acknowledges task- and deployment-dependent degradation. The method presents no unusual ethical concern, and reducing inference memory and computation could have positive environmental effects.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence supports identifying heads important under this particular local-cache intervention, but not the stronger interpretation that they are intrinsically “reasoning-critical” or the “primary drivers” of reasoning. These heads could instead be important for long-range generation generally. Comparisons against heads learned on non-reasoning generation, cross-model/head-set transfer, or matched-length instruction tasks would better establish reasoning specificity.

Statistical reliability is underdeveloped. Only point estimates from apparently single training runs are reported, with no seeds, confidence intervals, or variability across stochastic RL training. This matters especially for AIME24, where the test set has only 30 examples and each item changes accuracy by 3.3 percentage points.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the headline suggests. Table 2 obtains speedups by comparing RLKV at twice the batch size with the full model at roughly matched memory; it does not establish a comparable single-request latency gain or performance in a continuous-batching serving engine. Moreover, greedy-decoding accuracy changes across batch sizes, which deserves explanation.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The appendix reports datasets, major hyperparameters, hardware, prompts, and training costs, but no code or learned head masks are provided. Important details remain unclear, including exact checkpoint identifiers, gate parameterization and initialization, handling of zero-variance GRPO groups, curriculum ordering, head-count rounding, model-specific reward checking, and hyperparameter-selection protocol.

Training uses 128 sink plus 256 recent tokens with soft mixed attention, whereas deployment binarizes the ranking and retains only 16 plus 64 tokens. Although the empirical results partly validate this choice, the substantial train–inference mismatch is not isolated experimentally.

The baseline protocol modifies H2O and R-KV to use dynamic budgets. The authors motivate this choice and include a limited fixed-budget comparison, but clearer accounting of realized memory per generated sequence and evaluation under each baseline’s canonical configuration would make the fairness claim easier to verify.

Presentation contains minor inconsistencies and overstatements: for example, the text points to the wrong figure for error modes, includes references such as “Table Table 3,” and describes occasional gains over the full-cache baseline without uncertainty analysis. These do not undermine the main result but reduce polish.

strengths: Originality: RLKV offers a novel and intuitive adaptation of head-reallocation compression: outcome-based reinforcement learning learns per-head gates, rather than identifying heads through retrieval proxies or teacher-forced output matching. The continuous-gate training followed by top-k head selection is simple and practically relevant.

Soundness: The empirical study is broad, covering three reasoning models, four reasoning benchmarks, four MMLU-Pro subsets, and a 70K-context LongReason evaluation. Complete numerical results show that RLKV generally provides a better accuracy–compression frontier than H2O, R-KV, DuoAttention, and KVZip, especially around 40–60% head sparsity.

Significance: The paper addresses an important deployment bottleneck for long chain-of-thought generation. The SGLang dual-cache implementation demonstrates that the memory savings can translate into system-level benefits: on Llama-3.1-8B-R1/Math500, 40% sparsity gives 1.56x speedup with comparable accuracy, while 60% gives 2.06x speedup with a moderate accuracy loss.

The adaptive penalty and self-distillation mechanisms address a clearly identified optimization failure caused by sparse correctness rewards competing with dense L1 regularization. The component ablations, penalty sweep, and sink/local-window ablation provide useful supporting evidence.

The analyses distinguish RLKV heads from retrieval and random heads through intervention, examine compression-induced error modes, and report response-length effects. These experiments go beyond aggregate benchmark accuracy and offer useful hypotheses about reasoning-model compression.

Presentation is generally clear and polished, with a coherent motivation, understandable method, extensive appendices, full result tables, and concrete training and serving details. The limitations and impact sections honestly acknowledge severe degradation at 80% sparsity, static rather than query-adaptive gates, engine limitations, and possible task-dependent performance loss.
The computational requirements are manageable for follow-up work: only the small gate set is trained, and reported training costs are 22–40 GPU-hours per model rather than full-model post-training.
weaknesses: Soundness/statistics: All results appear to come from one head-discovery run and one evaluation run, with no confidence intervals or seed analysis despite stochastic GRPO training and explicitly acknowledged SGLang nondeterminism. Several highlighted improvements are only 1–3 percentage points; AIME24 has 30 examples, so a 6.7-point gain is just two questions. Claims that compressed models surpass full attention therefore lack adequate statistical support.

The mechanistic language is too strong. Optimizing jointly interacting gates and then showing that compressing the highest-ranked group hurts accuracy establishes a useful predictive intervention, but it does not show that individual heads are inherently the “primary carriers” of reasoning, control termination, or are uniquely essential. Gate rankings may reflect redundancy, co-adaptation, the chosen local window, and the specific training distribution. Stability of selected heads across seeds, datasets, and independently trained checkpoints is not measured.

The necessity of reinforcement learning is insufficiently isolated. The paper compares against existing methods with different objectives, but not against simpler outcome-aware alternatives such as per-head perturbation search, supervised optimization on verified trajectories, or gate optimization using teacher-forced sequence loss on the same 3,000 examples. Thus, the results support RLKV as a method but not the broader claim that rollout rewards are the only reliable signal.

The reported “KV cache reduction” is frequently equated with the fraction of heads assigned compressed caches. Actual memory reduction is smaller and sequence-dependent because compressed heads retain 16 sink plus 64 local tokens. Per-benchmark measured peak memory, rather than nominal head sparsity, is not reported, complicating equal-memory comparison and the central 20–60% reduction claim.

The baseline-budget protocol is confusing and partly oracle-dependent in its description. The main appendix describes an online budget growing with current sequence length, whereas Appendix F defines per-sample budgets using the full-attention response length. The latter is unavailable in real deployment. A clear online algorithm and comparisons at measured peak memory are needed to establish fairness.

System evidence is limited to one model, one benchmark, one GPU type, and a special serving setup that changes concurrency from 150 to 375 across sparsity levels. No latency distribution, peak-memory measurement, quality-adjusted throughput, or end-to-end comparison against competing compression implementations is given. Moreover, the 2.06x headline point loses 5.6 accuracy points, so it is not itself near-lossless.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript provides many hyperparameters but no code or artifact, exact checkpoint identifiers for every model, sampled training-example IDs, random seeds, gate initialization/constraint parameterization, exact verifier reward definition, or custom Triton/SGLang implementation. These omissions are material because reproducing the method requires modifying both training attention and a dual-pool inference engine.

Training uses a 128+256 local window but evaluation uses 16+64, and continuous mixed attention during optimization is discretized to binary top-k gates at inference. Although downstream results indicate this can work, these substantial train–test relaxations are not directly ablated, leaving unclear whether the learned scores remain optimal for the actual deployed operator.

The training set is filtered from DeepScaleR using each model's own successful generations, but the paper provides no overlap or contamination audit against Math500, AIME24, GSM8K, and other evaluations. Since mathematical benchmarks also guide hyperparameter and ablation choices, the breadth of out-of-distribution generalization is less convincing than presented.

The ethics discussion is adequate for a low-risk compression method and appropriately notes quality degradation, but it remains generic. Compression-induced silent errors and heterogeneous effects are evaluated only on math, code, and selected knowledge tasks; risks in safety-critical or demographic settings are not studied, so deployment claims should remain circumscribed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: reasoning-model generations are long and appear substantially more sensitive to KV-cache compression than instruction-model generations.

The proposed combination of frozen-model head gates, outcome-based GRPO optimization, L1 sparsification, adaptive penalty weighting, and self-distillation sampling is technically plausible and reasonably lightweight (reported as 22–40 A100 GPU-hours per model).

The empirical study is broader than average: three reasoning models, math, code, knowledge, and 70K-context evaluations; comparisons across several compression levels; component and window-size ablations; complete numerical tables; and analyses of failure types and generation lengths.

The SGLang integration provides useful system-level evidence rather than reporting cache size alone. On one model and workload, moderate sparsity gives a reported 1.56× speedup without an accuracy decrease, suggesting practical value.

The manuscript is generally organized and clearly motivated. It includes relevant implementation details, a limitations section acknowledging static gates and high-compression degradation, and an adequate impact statement with no evident unresolved ethical concern. weaknesses: Soundness: the evidence supports identifying heads that are sensitive to this particular local-attention intervention, but not the stronger interpretation that these heads are the “primary carriers” of reasoning or CoT consistency. The main sensitivity experiment is partly circular: heads optimized to retain full attention under the reward objective are ranked by their learned gates and then shown to be especially damaging when compressed.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. The mixed-attention gates and head-reallocation framework closely follow prior work; the principal novelty is replacing static or teacher-forced objectives with RL and adding stabilization heuristics. Especially relevant head-level methods cited in the paper, including Fu et al. and PruLong, are not included as baselines, making the improvement over the closest alternatives unclear.

The “20–60% near-lossless” headline is based on selecting a different sparsity threshold after observing each model–benchmark pair. Complete results show substantial degradation at 60% on many settings and near-total collapse at 80%. At the claimed maximum 60% setting in the speed table, accuracy falls from 79.4% to 73.8%, which is not near-lossless.

The system evidence is narrow and somewhat difficult to interpret: it covers one model, one benchmark, and one A100 configuration; concurrency changes from 150 to 375 across conditions; measured memory consumption is not reported; and the stated 2.06× speedup differs from the throughput ratio implied by the same table. A fixed-quality or fixed-concurrency comparison would better support the deployment claim.

Statistical reliability is insufficient. Results appear to come from single runs without confidence intervals or variability across training seeds. This is particularly problematic for AIME24, which has only 30 examples, where one answer changes accuracy by 3.3 points and several claimed improvements are only one or two examples.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful hyperparameter details: no code or trained gate artifacts are provided, some exact checkpoint identities are unclear, evaluation depends on custom Triton kernels and a modified SGLang implementation, and the authors acknowledge nondeterministic SGLang accuracy without quantifying it.

The evaluation is restricted to small 4B–8B distilled reasoning models. It does not establish that the learned head sparsity or training procedure scales to larger models, different attention architectures, or deployment distributions. Cross-task transfer is tested, but cross-model transfer is not.

Presentation is mostly clear, but several key plots are overly dense and hard to read, and the manuscript contains noticeable typographical and terminology issues. More importantly, the distinction between causal functional interpretation and intervention-specific compression sensitivity is not maintained consistently.

strengths: Soundness: The central practical result is supported by broad evaluation across three reasoning models, four reasoning benchmarks, four MMLU-Pro domains, and a 70K-context benchmark. RLKV generally provides a better accuracy–compression frontier than H2O, R-KV, DuoAttention, and KVZip, especially at moderate sparsity.

Significance: Head-level cache allocation is useful because it reduces memory while preserving complete histories for selected heads. The SGLang implementation demonstrates practical value, reaching 1.56× speedup at 40% sparsity with essentially unchanged Math500 accuracy and 2.06× at 60% sparsity with a larger accuracy loss.

Originality: Using outcome-based RL as a probe for cache sensitivity during autoregressive reasoning is a meaningful departure from retrieval proxies and teacher-forced objectives. The adaptive penalty and self-distillation mechanisms address a concrete instability caused by sparse rewards competing with dense regularization.

Presentation: The paper clearly motivates the failure modes of token dropping and retrieval-oriented head selection. The main comparisons, head-sensitivity intervention, error analysis, window-size study, and component ablations form a coherent empirical narrative.

Reproducibility and limitations: The appendix reports training data construction, optimization settings, cache-window sizes, hardware, training cost, prompts, evaluation engines, and baseline modifications. It also candidly acknowledges static gates, severe degradation at extreme sparsity, and current SGLang limitations. The environmental motivation and risk of task-dependent accuracy degradation are appropriately discussed, with no evident major ethical concern.
weaknesses: The strongest mechanistic language is not fully established. The experiments show that certain heads require full historical KV access under this particular local-attention intervention, but this does not demonstrate that they are the intrinsic or primary “carriers” of reasoning or termination. Cross-seed stability, cross-task head overlap, and controls against generic head importance would make that interpretation much stronger.

The empirical uncertainty is underreported. Results come from one adapter-training run per setting, with no confidence intervals or seed variation despite stochastic GRPO training and acknowledged inference nondeterminism. This is particularly consequential for AIME24, where one problem changes accuracy by 3.3 points and several claimed gains are only one or two problems.

“Near-lossless” is not formally defined and Table 1 selects different sparsity levels for different model–task pairs. At 60% sparsity, several complete-table results suffer substantial losses, so the headline claim of near-lossless 20–60% reduction should be qualified as task- and model-dependent rather than a uniform operating range.

The ablations are narrow: the RL stabilization components are studied only on Qwen-2.5-7B-R1/Math500, while the window study and serving benchmark use only Llama-3.1-8B-R1/Math500. The reported 2.06× result also changes concurrency across sparsity levels and retains a notable accuracy drop, so it does not establish the same speedup at fixed workload or uniformly near-lossless quality.

Some details needed for independent reproduction remain unclear, including the gate parameterization and initialization, handling of zero-variance reward groups, exact GRPO update conventions, and availability of the modified AReaL/SGLang code and Triton kernels. The construction of training data from DeepScaleR also warrants an explicit overlap or contamination audit against the mathematical evaluation sets.
